drivers: Recovery balance not provided — critical missing metric for readiness assessment

This month’s avg HR (148 bpm) is +14 bpm higher than last month’s (134 bpm), indicating sympathetic dominance or fatigue

readiness.guidance: Training intensity and volume must be reduced this week; focus on restoring autonomic balance before reintroducing structured work.

monthly_review.summary: September shows a dramatic drop in volume and shift toward higher-intensity running, accompanied by clear physiological stress markers — slower average pace, elevated HR, reduced efficiency, and erratic cadence.
monthly_review.highlight: The 20 spm cadence drop — from 149 in August to 129 in September — is the most notable finding, and aligns with elevated HR, higher aerobic TE, and a 90 spm outlier run, strongly indicating neuromuscular fatigue rather than fitness gain.

goal_tracker.message: Chasing last month’s volume is inadvisable: recovery indicators are compromised, and the abrupt drop in runs and cadence signals accumulated fatigue — not available capacity. Prioritizing readiness over distance is the correct call.

insights.title: Cadence collapse correlates with HR elevation and aerobic decoupling
insights.body: Average cadence fell 20 spm (149 → 129) while avg HR rose 14 bpm (134 → 148) and aerobic TE increased 0.6 points — all observed across the same monthly shift. The 90 spm run on 2026-09-06 (10.7 km, HR 158, TE 5.0) confirms this is not pacing strategy but fatigue-driven stride shortening and inefficiency.

insights.title: Improved running economy masks underlying strain
insights.body: Running economy improved from 14.12 to 13.12 ml/kg/km (lower = better), yet this coincides with higher HR, lower cadence, and worse aerobic TE — suggesting the improvement stems from reduced output (e.g., walking breaks, very slow pacing on long run) rather than true physiological gain, as confirmed by the 12:22 min/km pace on 2026-09-06.

insights.title: Zone 4 dominance replaces foundational Zone 1/2 work
insights.body: Zone 4 effort jumped from 8% in August to 46% in September, while Zone 1 collapsed from 43% to just 1% — a near-total abandonment of easy aerobic stimulus, despite declining endurance metrics (longest run dropped from 12.0 km to 10.7 km, and aerobic TE worsened).

recommendations.action: Zone 1 only: 45-min walk or very easy jog (HR ≤ 120 bpm) on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday — no pace target, stop if HR rises above 122 bpm for >60 sec
recommendations.reason: To re-establish parasympathetic tone and reduce sympathetic drive evidenced by elevated HR and cadence collapse

recommendations.action: Complete a 10-min seated HRV breathing session (5s in / 5s out) each morning before coffee, tracked via Garmin breathwork app
recommendations.reason: HRV is missing from dataset but required for readiness assessment; intentional coherence practice is the highest-leverage intervention when HRV data is unavailable

recommendations.action: Skip all running Sept 10–13; substitute with 20-min foam rolling + 10-min dynamic mobility (focus: hips, calves, thoracic spine)
recommendations.reason: The 10.7 km run on Sept 6 at 12:22 min/km and 158 bpm with 5.0% aerobic TE reflects severe fatigue — 4 days of zero-impact recovery is necessary to interrupt downward spiral

risk_flags.evidence: Cadence dropped 20 spm MoM; one run at 90 spm with HR 158 bpm and aerobic TE 5.0% — far outside historical norms (min TE was 1.0 on 2026-08-08)
risk_flags.action: Immediate cessation of all Zone 3+ efforts and cadence monitoring on every run

risk_flags.evidence: Avg HR increased +14 bpm MoM without corresponding pace increase (pace slowed), and aerobic TE rose +0.6 — classic signs of sympathetic nervous system dominance
risk_flags.action: Prioritise sleep consistency (target ≥7h, <30-min variability) and morning HR checks before training

weekly_focus.description: Shift emphasis from output (km, pace, zones) to input regulation (HR control, breath, movement quality) to restore HRV responsiveness and neuromuscular coordination.
